seoDescription: Discover the power and potential of supercapacitors by watching the build and launch of an electric rocket powered by these unique components. This project explores the differences between batteries, regular capacitors, and supercapacitors, demonstrating their distinct energy density and charge/discharge rates. See how six 3V supercapacitors are wired in series to power a 500-watt brushless motor, and follow the design, build, and flight testing process, including a custom parachute deployment system.

summary:
## Core Concepts: Capacitors vs. Batteries

- **Energy Storage**: Batteries store energy **chemically**, while capacitors store it as **static electricity**. This allows capacitors to charge and discharge much faster.
- **Energy Density**: There is a clear hierarchy in energy density:
    - **Battery**: Highest energy density, provides long-lasting power.
    - **Supercapacitor**: Medium energy density; stores significantly more energy than a regular capacitor but less than a battery.
    - **Regular Capacitor**: Lowest energy density; discharges almost instantly under load.

## The Project: Supercapacitor Rocket

A rocket was designed and built to test the viability of using supercapacitors for high-power, short-duration flight. The goal was to power a **500W brushless motor** with a pack of six supercapacitors to see how high it could fly.

## Bench Testing and System Design

- **Power Source**: 6 x 3V supercapacitors were wired in **series** to create a single 18V power pack.
- **Control System**: A 30A Electronic Speed Controller (ESC) was used to control the brushless motor.
- **Test Results**: The system successfully powered the motor unloaded. The ESC's low voltage cutoff was triggered at **6.4V**, at which point the motor stopped receiving power.

> [!IMPORTANT]
A small separate battery was used to power the servo tester for controlling the ESC during the bench test, but it did not provide any power to the main motor system.

## Rocket Airframe and Systems

- **Motor Position**: The motor and propeller were placed at the top in a **tractor configuration**. This design choice was made to avoid ground clearance issues and potential interference with a launch guide rail, not for stability reasons.

> [!NOTE]
The video debunks the "pendulum rocket fallacy," clarifying that the thrust unit's position (top or bottom) does not inherently dictate stability.

- **Component Placement**: The heavy supercapacitors were also placed near the top, close to the motor. This contributes to a stable center of gravity and allows for shorter, more efficient high-current power wires.
- **Charging**: An **XT60 connector** was integrated into the fuselage, allowing the supercapacitor bank to be fully charged from a standard LiPo battery in a matter of seconds.
- **Parachute System**: A custom, servo-actuated parachute system was designed.
    - It is located at the bottom of the rocket.
    - The entire fin section is split in two and clamped to the body tube by a rubber band.
    - A remote signal activates a servo, which pulls a pin and releases the rubber band, causing the fin halves to separate and deploy the parachute.

## Flight Testing and Results

- **Version 1**: The initial rocket design proved to be aerodynamically unstable and crashed on its first test flights.
- **Version 2**: After rebuilding, the V2 rocket featured a stronger top section and a more rigid fin clamping system to prevent the airframe from twisting in flight.
- **Performance**: The V2 rocket achieved multiple successful flights, reaching an estimated maximum altitude of **60-80 meters** (just under 200 feet).
- **Failures**: Flight testing was not without issues. One flight had a dangerously delayed parachute deployment, and the final flight ended in a crash when the parachute failed to deploy entirely, destroying the fin section on impact.

## Key Takeaways

- Supercapacitors are a viable power source for high-discharge, short-duration applications like model rocketry.
- Their ability to be **recharged in seconds** proved to be a major advantage, allowing for multiple launches in a short period with a single charging battery.
- The project highlights the iterative nature of engineering, where the failure of the V1 rocket led to critical design improvements for the successful V2.

## Capacitors vs. Batteries: A Demonstration

Oh, if you've ever taken a look inside an electronic product before or have some general knowledge of electronics, you've probably seen or heard of a capacitor. A capacitor stores electrical energy similar to a battery but in a very different way. A battery stores energy within a chemical, which can then be converted into electrical energy to power whatever you want, whereas a capacitor actually stores the electrical energy in the form of static electricity. What this means is that it can be charged and discharged much faster than a battery can, but there are some disadvantages.

So here I have a motor and the propeller strapped to a piece of wood so hopefully it doesn't fly away. And I have a battery cell and a capacitor. Now what I can do is I can wire up this battery to power the electric motor. And I should also be able to use the capacitor to output its electrical energy to power the motor. Oh, that's a... that's a capacitor fully discharged. So from that quick test, you can tell that a capacitor has far less energy density than a battery.

## Introducing Supercapacitors

And this is where super capacitors come in. A super capacitor works in a similar way to a regular capacitor, but it's a bit more advanced and can store far more energy. Not quite as much as a battery, but it can be charged and discharged pretty quickly. So how about we wire this up to the motor?

Okay, it's a bit of a dodgy connection just holding the wires like this, but that should give you a pretty good idea that super capacitors have far more energy density than regular capacitors. In fact, the super capacitor has enough energy to power a small plane like this, which can be charged up in a matter of seconds and powers this plane for quite a bit of time.

Now this plane is pretty cool, but I still don't think it's using the full potential of a super capacitor. So I think it's time to step it up a notch, or maybe a bit more. I'm going to use six of these super capacitors to power a 500 watt brushless motor using a large propeller to see how high I can launch an electric rocket. Let's go!

## Bench Testing the Rocket Power System

Right, so before I shorten the wires and make everything a bit neater, I just want to give it a quick run just to check whether, first of all, nothing is wired up wrong and also that these super capacitors can power the motor. So that's just telling the speed control what to do and I should be able to short these into a battery. I highly do not recommend this, but I haven't put a connector on this just yet. ## Rocket Design & Parachute System

Okay, so here we have it, the finished super capacitor rocket. At the top here, I have the motor and propeller, which is the thrust unit. The reason for it being at the top is not for stability reasons. It doesn't matter at what point on a rocket you have the thrust unit if you research the pendulum rocket fallacy. The reason why it's at the top and not the bottom is because with the propeller being at the bottom, there's clearance issues with the ground. I would need to build big fins to go around the side of the propeller, and also if I need to add any kind of guide rail system at the side of the rocket, the propeller must be well clear of that guide system. So basically have a no-go zone disk as the propeller rises up from the ground. So having it at the top just gets rid of any clearance issues.

The motor is powered or controlled via this electronic speed controller. It's 30 amps and it... well, this is currently set up for about 18 volts, but it can run up to 25 volts, I believe. And then obviously, we have the whole super capacitor unit. There's six super capacitors in total. The reason for this is that super capacitors are usually quite low voltage. These are rated for 3 volts each, so six of them in series is 18 volts. These are all obviously wired into the speed control and directly to the motor. Having all the mass at the top is what you want for a stable rocket, and also having these super capacitors so close to the motor means I should be able to deliver the power a lot better without having some thick gauge wires going down to the bottom.

Now you can probably see this yellow thing in here. This is actually the connector where I charge up the rocket. Now moving down the rocket is the parachute deployment system. Now I've built it into the fin system, and the way it deploys is this whole fin section is split into two halves and there's a rubber band that holds these two halves together and that clamps it to the tube.
